lessons.title: What Is a Fruit Concentrate? Benefits and Uses
lessons.body:
A fruit concentrate is simply fruit juice with most of the water removed. If you start with 10 litres of fresh mango juice and remove 7 litres of water, you end up with about 3 litres of thick, syrupy concentrate. That concentrate still contains all the natural sugars, acids, colours, and flavours of the original fruitâjust in a smaller volume. In Africa, where mangoes and pineapples often rot in the field during harvest season, concentrates solve two big problems: they reduce spoilage and make transport cheaper. A 20-litre bucket of concentrate can make 100 litres of ready-to-drink juice, so you can sell far more product from the same harvest.

Concentrates are used in three main ways. First, for juice sales: you mix concentrate with clean water, add sugar if needed, and sell as fresh juice. Second, as ingredients for other businesses: bakeries, ice cream makers, and yoghurt producers buy concentrate to flavour their products. Third, for home use: a spoonful of pineapple concentrate can sweeten tea or porridge. Because concentrate is thick and acidic, it resists spoilage better than fresh juice. If you keep it in a clean, airtight container in a cool, dark place, it can last 3â6 months without refrigeration. That means you can process fruit during the glut and sell all year round.

To make concentrate, you need a few basic tools: a juicer or blender, a large pot or a solar dryer, a fine mesh strainer or muslin cloth, clean glass bottles or food-grade plastic containers, and a refractometer if you want to measure sugar levels (Brix). A simple refractometer costs about $20â$40 and helps you keep quality consistent. The key is to remove water without burning the juice. You can do this by slow boiling, vacuum evaporation, or solar drying. Each method has trade-offs in cost, speed, and flavour retention.

One important note: concentrate is not the same as squash or cordial. Squash has added sugar and preservatives; concentrate is pure fruit. When you sell concentrate, you are selling a raw ingredient that your customers can dilute to their own taste. This makes it a flexible product for both households and small businesses.

lessons.title: Evaporation Methods: Open Pot, Vacuum, and Solar
lessons.body:
Evaporation is the heart of concentrate making. You need to remove water from juice without destroying flavour, colour, or nutrients. Three methods work in an African setting: open pot boiling, vacuum evaporation, and solar evaporation. Each has a different cost and quality outcome.

Open pot boiling is the simplest and cheapest. Use a wide, heavy-bottomed stainless steel pot. Pour in fresh juiceâmango, pineapple, or a mix. Heat over a medium fire, stirring constantly with a wooden spoon to prevent burning. Bring to a gentle simmer (about 90â95Â°C) and keep stirring. Water will rise as steam. For every 10 litres of juice, you can expect to remove 6â7 litres of water in 2â3 hours. The concentrate is ready when it coats the back of the spoon or when a drop on a cold plate stays thick. The downside: heat can dull the fresh flavour and darken the colour. To reduce this, keep the temperature below boiling and stir often. Never let it scorchâburnt concentrate tastes bitter and cannot be fixed.

Vacuum evaporation is faster and preserves flavour better. You need a vacuum pump and a sealed vessel, which can cost $200â$500. The juice boils at 40â60Â°C under vacuum, so delicate flavours survive. This method is best if you plan to sell to bakeries or ice cream makers who demand high-quality concentrate. In many African cities, you can rent time on a vacuum evaporator at a food processing incubator or university lab. If you cannot afford your own, consider a shared facility.

Solar evaporation uses the sun. Build a solar dryer with a black tray inside a glass-covered box. Pour juice into the tray at 1â2 cm depth. The sun heats the juice and water evaporates through vents. On a hot day (30â35Â°C), 10 litres of juice can reduce to 3 litres in 6â8 hours. Solar evaporation is slow but free and retains more nutrients than open boiling. However, it risks contamination from dust and insects, so cover the tray with a fine mesh. Also, if the weather turns cloudy, the juice can ferment. Use solar evaporation only for small batches and when you have reliable sunshine.

Choose your method based on your budget, batch size, and target market. For home sales, open pot works. For business-to-business, vacuum is best. For a low-cost, off-grid option, solar is viable with care.

lessons.title: Making Mango and Pineapple Concentrates
lessons.body:
Mango and pineapple are two of Africa's most abundant fruits, and both make excellent concentrates. The process is similar but each fruit has quirks. Follow these steps for a 10-litre batch of fresh juice, which will yield about 3 litres of concentrate.

For mango concentrate: choose ripe but firm mangoesâoverripe fruit gives a dull flavour. Wash, peel, and cut the flesh away from the stone. Blend the flesh with a little water (1 cup water per 4 cups mango) to help extraction. Strain through a muslin cloth or fine sieve to remove fibre. You should get about 6â7 litres of thick juice from 10 kg of mangoes. Pour the juice into a pot and simmer gently, stirring constantly. Mango juice burns easily because of its natural sugars. Keep the heat low and stir every 30 seconds. After 2â3 hours, the volume will drop to about 2â3 litres. The concentrate should be thick like honey. Add a pinch of citric acid (1/4 teaspoon per litre) to brighten the flavour and help preservation. Bottle hot into clean glass jars.

For pineapple concentrate: select ripe pineapples with a sweet aroma. Peel, remove the eyes, and cut into chunks. Blend without adding waterâpineapple is juicy. Strain to remove pulp. You should get 7â8 litres of juice from 10 kg of fruit. Pineapple juice is more acidic than mango, so it foams during boiling. Use a tall pot to avoid overflow. Simmer gently, skimming off foam with a spoon. After 2â3 hours, you will have 2â3 litres of concentrate. Pineapple concentrate is very tart; you may add sugar later when reconstituting. Do not add sugar during concentrationâit can cause crystallisation. Bottle hot.

For both fruits, test the concentrate by cooling a spoonful. It should be thick and syrupy, not watery. If it is still thin, continue simmering. Record your yield: for every 10 litres of juice, you should get 2.5â3.5 litres of concentrate. If you get less, you may have boiled too hard and lost flavour. If more, it is under-concentrated and will spoil faster. Store in sterilised bottles with airtight lids. Label with fruit type and date. Use within 6 months.

lessons.title: Packaging and Storing Concentrates
lessons.body:
Concentrate is a high-value product, so packaging must protect it from air, light, moisture, and contamination. Poor packaging ruins months of work. Follow these practical steps for small-scale African producers.

First, sterilise your containers. Glass bottles or jars are best because they do not react with acid. Wash them with hot soapy water, rinse, then place in an oven at 120Â°C for 15 minutes or boil in water for 10 minutes. Let them dry upside down on a clean cloth. For plastic, use food-grade PET or HDPE containers. Never use old cooking oil bottlesâthey harbour bacteria and smells. If you are selling to businesses, use 1-litre or 5-litre food-grade buckets with tight lids.

Second, fill hot. Pour concentrate into containers while it is still hot (above 80Â°C). This creates a vacuum seal as it cools, killing most microbes. Leave 1 cm headspace. Seal immediately with a new lid. For glass jars, you can use a simple metal lid that pops down when sealed. For plastic buckets, use a rubber gasket lid. After sealing, turn the jar upside down for 2 minutes to sterilise the lid, then turn upright.

Third, label clearly. Include: fruit type (e.g., Mango Concentrate), date of production, batch number, and instructions for reconstitution (e.g., âMix 1 part concentrate with 4 parts waterâ). If you sell to other businesses, add your contact details and a âbest beforeâ date 6 months from production. Use waterproof labels or write directly on the lid with a permanent marker.

Fourth, store properly. Keep in a cool, dark placeâa cupboard away from the stove, or a cellar. Ideal temperature is 10â20Â°C. Do not expose to direct sunlight; UV light destroys colour and vitamins. Once opened, store in the refrigerator and use within 2 weeks. If you see mould, a fizzy smell, or a changed colour, discard the whole batch. Do not scoop out mould and use the restâtoxins spread invisibly.

For transport to markets, pack bottles in crates with newspaper or straw to prevent breakage. If you are selling at a distant market, consider using 5-litre plastic jerrycans instead of glass to reduce weight and breakage. Always keep a sample from each batch so you can trace any quality problem.

lessons.title: Reconstituting Concentrates for Juice Sales
lessons.body:
Reconstituting means adding water back to concentrate to make ready-to-drink juice. This is where you turn a thick syrup into a sellable beverage. The key is to get the ratio right so your juice tastes good and your costs are controlled. A standard ratio for most fruit concentrates is 1 part concentrate to 4 parts clean water. So 1 litre of concentrate makes 5 litres of juice. But this varies by fruit and customer preference. Mango concentrate is sweet, so you might use 1:5. Pineapple is tart, so 1:4 or even 1:3 if you want a strong taste.

Start by measuring. Use a clean measuring jug. Pour 1 litre of concentrate into a 10-litre bucket. Add 4 litres of safe water. Stir well with a long spoon. Taste. If it is too thick, add more water 100 ml at a time. If too thin, add more concentrate. For a consistent product, use a refractometer to check Brix. Most ready-to-drink juices are 10â12 Brix. Your concentrate might be 60â70 Brix. So you need to dilute until you hit 10â12 Brix. Without a refractometer, rely on taste and a simple rule: the juice should taste like fresh fruit, not like syrup.

Next, adjust sweetness. Concentrate has natural sugars, but customers often expect a sweeter juice. Add sugar syrup, not dry sugar, to avoid gritty texture. Make syrup by dissolving 1 kg of sugar in 1 litre of hot water. Cool it, then add to the juice. Start with 100 ml of syrup per 5 litres of juice. Taste and adjust. You can also add a pinch of citric acid (1/4 teaspoon per 5 litres) to brighten flavour. For pineapple, a squeeze of fresh lime helps.

Finally, chill and serve. If you are selling from a cooler, keep the juice at 4Â°C or add ice. For immediate sale, pour into clean cups or bottles. If you are bottling for later, pasteurise by heating to 75Â°C for 15 seconds, then hot-fill into sterilised bottles. Label with date and âkeep refrigeratedâ. Sell within 3 days if unpasteurised, or 2 weeks if pasteurised. Always calculate your cost: if 1 litre of concentrate costs you $2 to make, and you get 5 litres of juice, your cost per litre is $0.40. Add cups, labour, and transport, then set a price that gives you at least 50% profit.

lessons.title: Selling Concentrates to Other Businesses
lessons.body:
Selling concentrate to other businesses is often more profitable than selling juice to consumers. You sell in bulk, you don't need to bottle or chill, and you get repeat orders. Your customers include bakeries, ice cream makers, yoghurt producers, hotels, restaurants, and other juice vendors. They buy concentrate because it saves them time, reduces waste, and gives consistent flavour year-round.

To start, identify your local buyers. Visit bakeries and ask if they use fruit flavourings. Many use artificial syrups; your natural concentrate is a premium upgrade. Ice cream makers love mango and pineapple concentrate because it adds real fruit taste. Yoghurt producers can stir it in for fruit-on-the-bottom cups. Hotels and restaurants use it for cocktails, smoothies, and sauces. Make a simple list of 10 potential buyers within 20 km of your production site.

Next, prepare samples. Put 200 ml of concentrate in a clean, labelled bottle. Include a one-page sheet with: fruit type, Brix level (e.g., 65 Brix), ingredients (100% fruit, no preservatives), shelf life (6 months unopened), and reconstitution ratio (1:4). Offer a free sample so they can test it in their own kitchen. Follow up after 3 days. Ask for feedback on taste, thickness, and packaging. Be ready to adjust your productâsome bakers want a thicker concentrate, some want it less sweet.

Price your concentrate fairly. Calculate your cost per litre: fruit, labour, fuel, bottles, and labels. For example, if 10 kg of mangoes costs $5, and you get 3 litres of concentrate, your raw material cost is $1.67 per litre. Add $0.50 for packaging and $0.50 for labour and fuel, total $2.67. Sell at $4â$5 per litre to a business. That gives you 50â80% profit. Offer a discount for bulk orders (e.g., 10 litres for $40).

Deliver reliably. Agree on a delivery scheduleâweekly or bi-weekly. Use clean, food-grade containers. Always include a batch number and date. Ask for payment on delivery or within 7 days. Keep records of each sale. As you grow, you can buy larger equipment and hire help. Remember: one bakery that buys 5 litres per week is worth more than 50 one-time customers. Build relationships, be consistent, and your concentrate business will grow.

quiz.q: What is a fruit concentrate?
options: A) Fruit juice with added sugar and preservatives
B) Fruit juice with most of the water removed
C) A type of squash or cordial
quiz.explanation: Concentrate is juice with water removed, leaving a thick syrup.

quiz.q: How much concentrate can you typically get from 10 litres of fresh juice?
quiz.explanation: Removing 6â7 litres of water leaves about 3 litres of concentrate.

quiz.q: Which tool helps measure sugar levels in concentrate?
quiz.explanation: A refractometer measures Brix, the sugar content.

quiz.q: What is a key benefit of concentrate over fresh juice?
options: B) It lasts longer without refrigeration
C) It is cheaper to produce
quiz.explanation: Concentrate resists spoilage and can last 3â6 months unrefrigerated.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a common use of fruit concentrate?
options: C) As a substitute for fresh fruit in salads
quiz.explanation: Concentrate is a liquid ingredient, not a replacement for fresh fruit pieces.

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of vacuum evaporation over open pot boiling?
options: D) It works faster without heat
quiz.explanation: Vacuum evaporation boils at lower temperatures, retaining delicate flavours.

quiz.q: At what temperature does juice boil under vacuum?
quiz.explanation: Lower pressure allows boiling at 40â60Â°C, preserving quality.

quiz.q: What is a risk of solar evaporation?
options: C) Contamination from dust and insects
quiz.explanation: Open solar trays can be contaminated unless covered with fine mesh.

quiz.q: Why should you stir mango juice constantly during open pot evaporation?
quiz.explanation: Mango juice has high sugar and burns easily if not stirred.

quiz.q: What should you add to mango concentrate to brighten flavour and aid preservation?
quiz.explanation: A pinch of citric acid enhances tartness and acts as a preservative.

quiz.q: Why should you not add sugar to pineapple juice before concentrating?
options: A) It makes it too sweet
quiz.explanation: Added sugar can crystallise during concentration, ruining texture.

quiz.q: How much concentrate should you expect from 10 kg of mangoes?
quiz.explanation: 10 kg mangoes yields about 6â7 litres juice, reducing to 2â3 litres concentrate.

quiz.q: What is the best way to sterilise glass bottles for concentrate?
options: B) Boil in water for 10 minutes
C) Wipe with a dry cloth
quiz.explanation: Boiling kills microbes; oven heating at 120Â°C also works.

quiz.q: Why should you fill containers while concentrate is still hot?
options: B) It creates a vacuum seal
quiz.explanation: Hot filling and sealing creates a vacuum that inhibits microbial growth.

quiz.q: What information should be on a concentrate label?
options: B) Fruit type, date, batch number, and reconstitution ratio
D) Your name and phone number only
quiz.explanation: Full traceability and usage instructions are essential for food safety.

quiz.q: Where should you store unopened concentrate?
options: B) In a cool, dark place
quiz.explanation: Cool, dark conditions (10â20Â°C) preserve quality and prevent spoilage.

quiz.q: What should you do if you see mould on concentrate?
options: A) Scoop it off and use the rest
quiz.explanation: Mould toxins spread invisibly; the entire batch is unsafe.

quiz.q: What is the standard reconstitution ratio for most fruit concentrates?
options: A) 1 part concentrate to 1 part water
B) 1 part concentrate to 2 parts water
C) 1 part concentrate to 4 parts water
D) 1 part concentrate to 10 parts water
quiz.explanation: 1:4 is a common starting ratio, yielding 5 litres of juice from 1 litre concentrate.

quiz.q: What Brix range is typical for ready-to-drink juice?
quiz.explanation: Most palatable juices are around 10â12 Brix.

quiz.q: Why should you add sugar as a syrup rather than dry sugar when reconstituting?
quiz.explanation: Dry sugar may not dissolve fully, leaving a gritty mouthfeel.

quiz.q: How long can unpasteurised reconstituted juice last if refrigerated?
quiz.explanation: Unpasteurised juice should be used within 3 days when kept cold.

quiz.q: What is a key advantage of selling concentrate to businesses?
options: A) You need to bottle and chill it
B) You get repeat bulk orders
C) You sell in small quantities
quiz.explanation: Businesses buy in bulk regularly, providing steady income.

quiz.q: Which of these is a potential business buyer of fruit concentrate?
quiz.explanation: Bakeries use fruit concentrate for flavourings and fillings.

quiz.q: What should you include with a sample sent to a potential business buyer?
options: B) A one-page sheet with product details
quiz.explanation: Details like Brix, ingredients, shelf life, and ratio help buyers evaluate.

quiz.q: If 10 kg of mangoes costs $5 and yields 3 litres of concentrate, what is the raw material cost per litre?
quiz.explanation: $5 Ã· 3 litres = $1.67 per litre.

quiz.q: What is a fair profit margin when selling concentrate to a business?
quiz.explanation: A 50â80% margin covers costs and allows growth.

quiz.q: Why is one bakery buying 5 litres weekly better than 50 one-time customers?
options: A) It pays more per litre
B) It provides reliable repeat income
D) It is easier to deliver
quiz.explanation: Repeat business builds sustainable revenue and relationships.

quiz.q: What is the recommended headspace when filling concentrate into containers?
quiz.explanation: 1 cm allows for expansion and vacuum sealing without overflow.

quiz.q: Which fruit concentrate is naturally more tart and may need less added citric acid?
quiz.explanation: Pineapple is already acidic, so extra citric acid may not be needed.

quiz.q: What should you do after sealing a hot-filled jar?
options: A) Cool it in cold water immediately
B) Turn it upside down for 2 minutes
C) Open it to release steam
quiz.explanation: Inverting sterilises the lid and helps create a vacuum seal.
